summary: Defines changes to the DNS to support renumberable and aggregatable IPv6 addressing. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This was a plan to change how the Internet's address book stores the newer address numbers so they could be reorganized easily. It is no longer used.

subtitle: A Historic scheme that stored IPv6 addresses as chains of prefix records so networks could be renumbered easily.

tldr.problem: Keeping address information in the DNS was one obstacle to renumbering sites and providers in IPv4, and the same problem threatened IPv6 if each full address was stored in a single record.
tldr.mechanism: A new A6 record holds part of an IPv6 address plus a prefix length and the name of another record that supplies the leading bits. Reverse lookups use bit-string labels under IP6.ARPA and DNAME records to delegate on any bit boundary.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2874 proposed replacing RFC 1886. It is now marked Historic, and later RFCs have updated it.

facts.label: Recommended delegation depth
facts.value: One or two levels until more experience is gained

today: RFC 2874 is marked Historic. It updated RFC 1886 and has itself been updated by RFC 3152, RFC 3226, RFC 3363 and RFC 3364, so the A6 scheme it describes should not be treated as current.

sections.title: Why Renumbering Needs New DNS Records
sections.content:
The authors point to the maintenance of address information in the DNS as one of the obstacles that made site and provider renumbering infeasible in IP version 4. To store IPv6 addresses without blocking renumbering, the RFC defines four extensions.

  • A new record type, A6, maps a name to an IPv6 address, with indirection for the leading prefix bits.
  • Queries that do additional section processing for IPv4 addresses are redefined to handle IPv6 addresses as well.
  • A new domain, IP6.ARPA, supports lookups by IPv6 address.
  • A new prefix-delegation method relies on bit-string labels and DNAME records.

The memo proposes a replacement for the specification in RFC 1886 and a departure from current implementation practice, and expects that RFC 1886 will become Historic after a reasonable period.
sections.eli5: The goal is to make the Internet's address book easy to update when a whole neighborhood changes its numbers.

sections.title: The A6 Record
sections.content:
The A6 record is specific to the IN class and has type number 38. Its data has up to three parts: a prefix length (one octet, 0 to 128), an address suffix (exactly enough octets to hold 128 minus the prefix length bits, with zero pad bits) and a prefix name, a domain name that MUST NOT be compressed.

The name is absent when the prefix length is zero, and the suffix is absent when the prefix length is 128. A prefix length of zero means the record holds a complete address; otherwise the name points to other A6 records that supply the leading bits.
sections.eli5: An A6 record is a card with the last part of an address and a pointer to the card that has the first part.

sections.title: Building an Address From a Chain
sections.content:
To find the addresses of a name, a client MUST obtain one or more complete chains of A6 records. A chain starts with a record owned by the name, follows the prefix name in each record, and ends with a record whose prefix length is zero. Each bit of the address comes from the earliest record in the chain that validly covers that position. Several records at any level multiply the number of addresses formed.

If an A6 record with prefix length L1 refers to a name that owns a record with a larger prefix length L2, the offending record with the larger length MUST be ignored. A query for A6 also triggers additional section processing for the prefix names. If only some queries succeed, a client may get a non-empty but incomplete set of addresses, which the RFC says may be acceptable in many situations.

Existing query types that add address data (NS, MX, MB, AFSDB and RT) are redefined to add A, A6 and AAAA data, with A highest priority and AAAA lowest. Resolvers must also limit the work they do per request, including the number of DNS requests generated.
sections.eli5: To find the full address, follow the notes from card to card until you reach one with nothing left to look up, then glue the pieces together.

sections.title: Reverse Lookups With IP6.ARPA
sections.content:
Lookups keyed on an IPv6 address use a bit-string label, which compactly represents an arbitrary string of bits as one-bit domain labels. This allows records at any bit boundary. In the RFC's notation, \[x3FFE07C0004000090A0020FFFE812B32/128].IP6.ARPA. names a full 128-bit address.

Delegation uses DNAME records, an analogue of CNAME for a whole subtree, instead of zone cuts and NS records. The RFC says all address space delegations SHOULD use DNAME rather than NS, and suggests storing address and prefix data immediately below a label IP6. A client finds a name for an address by sending a PTR query with QCLASS=IN for the bit-string name under IP6.ARPA, then follows returned DNAME and NS records.

Because each zone is reached by DNAME, one zone can serve several parallel copies of an address space, such as a site with two providers, and survives renumbering unchanged.
sections.eli5: To find who lives at an address, you ask the big office, which says 'ask this smaller office', which says 'ask the next one', until someone knows.

sections.title: Transition From RFC 1886 and Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
Long chains cost more records and more lookups, and the records usually come from different zones that can fail independently. The records can exceed the space in a UDP response, and DNS Security checking costs more when different signature chains must be verified. Until more experience is gained, the RFC recommends limiting prefix delegations to one or two levels, starting with none and moving to a single level inside one zone.

To keep working with resolvers that only know AAAA records, zones can generate AAAA records automatically from their A6 data. A generated AAAA record's TTL MUST be no more than the minimum TTL of the A6 records used, and it MUST be signed if the zone is secure. Clients may be configurable in their A6 and AAAA order, but the default MUST be to try A6 first, then AAAA.

For reverse lookups, RFC 1886 used nibble labels under IP6.INT. The RFC recommends that, during a transition, implementations first look up the binary label in IP6.ARPA and, if that fails, try the nibble label in IP6.INT.
sections.eli5: While everyone switches to the new address book, the old one keeps working side by side, and people check the new one first.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Signing authority for the A6 records of an address is spread across the entities along its delegation path. DNS Security applies fully to bit-string labels and DNAME records, and checking name-to-address mappings is logically independent of checking address-to-name mappings, as in IPv4.

An incomplete but non-empty address set could be caused by selective interference with lookups. Clients could mitigate this by refusing to act on an incomplete set, or servers by listing all addresses in A6 records with prefix length 0. IANA assigned the A6 resource record the type value 38.
sections.eli5: Because the address is assembled from many cards, a trickster who hides one card could cause trouble, so careful clients check they got them all.

viz.caption: SITE X'S A6 RECORDS FROM THE RFC'S EXAMPLE (RFC 2874)

data.title: A chain of A6 records
data.code:
$ORIGIN X.EXAMPLE.
N            A6 64 ::1234:5678:9ABC:DEF0 SUBNET-1.IP6
SUBNET-1.IP6 A6 48 0:0:0:1::  IP6
IP6          A6 48 0::0       SUBSCRIBER-X.IP6.A.NET.
IP6          A6 48 0::0       SUBSCRIBER-X.IP6.B.NET.
